_doc: Machine-readable work plan. progress_watch.py reads this, executes `auto` items, dispatches `code` items to opencode in an isolated worktree, and only marks an item done when its `verify` command passes. Never tick an item by hand because it looks finished: record the evidence.

_kinds.auto: A command the watcher runs itself (idempotent, read-only or additive).
_kinds.code: A coding task the watcher dispatches to opencode, one deliverable per session.
_kinds.ops: A deployment/operations action; requires a passing `gate` before it may run.
_kinds.decision: Needs a human choice; the watcher only surfaces it.

items.title: Attribute the 426.9 ms single index scan (engine path) vs 56 ms (legacy path)
items.detail: MEASURED: engine path p50 452 ms of which one index scan is 426.9 ms; the legacy query::execute path returns the same 10 results for 56 ms. Research (apizio/t/sonar) ranks the likely causes: (1) large internal candidate limit, (2) multi-term disjunction / phrase / slop query shape, (3) poor pruning, (4) single-segment layout blocking search_with_executor. Instrument the candidate limit actually passed to Searcher::search, and the segment count, before changing anything.
items.verify: A per-stage timing line showing the candidate limit and segment count actually used, plus before/after p50 with nDCG@10 unchanged.
items.evidence: b84c324 merged as b84c324; tests: test result: ok. 0 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.00s; test result: ok. 4 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.28s; test resul

items.title: Pin the fast-mode graph-lane skip with a test
items.detail: Commit 245d20a makes fast mode skip the graph lane because it measured +261 ms p50 for -0.4 pt nDCG, but landed build-verified with no test. Add a test that a Fast-mode request does not run a lane exposing an expanding view, and that Auto/Deep still do.

items.title: Structure the crawled fleet into index-model packs
items.detail: Shard 0 export running with the shared LLM cache. Shards 1-3 queue behind it. Each shard has its own Tantivy index, so export reads it and writes a pack; repeated pages are free because the cache key includes the URL.
items.verify: pack-shard-{shard}/manifest.json exists with a record count > 0 and a failure count that is reported honestly (never hidden).

items.title: Deduplicate identical pages across the four fleet shards
items.detail: Shards are host-disjoint, so cross-shard duplicates are rare by construction; structuring repeats are already free because the LLM cache key includes the URL. Low priority: measure the duplicate rate over blob sha256 before spending anything on it.
items.verify: A measured duplicate rate reported; if it is negligible, close this item as not-worth-doing rather than leaving it open.

items.title: Import the fleet packs into the serving index and deploy
items.gate: SEARCH_DATA_DIR=<staging> target/release/agent0 eval run --set benchmarks/queries.corpus.jsonl --limit 10 --lanes none
items.detail: Blocked until the packs exist. The live site serves 19,255 pages while ~221,000 are on disk. Import into a STAGING data dir first and require nDCG@10 >= the current deployed 0.4913 before any swap; a corpus that answers worse is not progress.
items.verify: Staging eval nDCG@10 recorded, then the swap, then a live curl showing the new document count - never the other way round.

items.title: Decide the stored-fields question (headings/doc_type/language are indexed-not-stored)
items.detail: Read-back is lossy: all_docs rebuilds documents through a converter that hardcodes those fields, so they are searchable but not recoverable via export --raw. Options: a schema version bump with a re-index (correct, expensive), or a sidecar (cheap, one more artifact to keep consistent).
items.verify: A recorded decision with its cost, not an implicit drift.

items.title: Research the state of the art for fast sparse retrieval, early termination and candidate pruning
items.detail: Question: for a LOCAL index of 19k-231k documents sitting on one box, what are the current (2024-2026) best techniques to make a top-k lexical or learned-sparse query fast: early termination (WAND/BlockMax-WAND and successors), block-max and superblock pruning, candidate-limit sizing, segment layouts and query parallelism, and doc-side weighting (learned sparse) instead of query-side expansion. For each: how it works in one paragraph, what it costs, what it buys, and whether it applies to a Tantivy-backed engine. Cite every claim with a link to the paper or repo.
items.verify: references/research/index-algorithms.md exists, is at least 1500 characters, cites sources with links, and ends with a ranked list of techniques applicable to our engine.
items.evidence: references/research/index-algorithms.md (9,078 chars) - captured from the session transcript

items.title: Research why people choose particular search engines, and what that means for ours
items.detail: Question: why do people choose and stay with particular search engines (Google, Bing, Brave, DuckDuckGo, Kagi, Perplexity, Marginalia, and agent-native tools), and what makes them switch? Separate the factors: result quality, latency, privacy/trust, transparency and control, familiarity, price and lock-in, and the ability to verify or cite. For each factor, evidence and sources. Then the actionable half: which of these can a LOCAL, agent-native engine with real crawled data and honest empty states actually win on, and what concrete features would it take? Cite sources with links.
items.verify: references/research/search-engine-choice.md exists, is at least 1500 characters, cites sources, and ends with concrete, buildable recommendations.

Implement it, and measure before/after with the eval harness.

items.title: Watch crawl throughput against the resources actually available, and act
items.detail: MEASURED ISSUE: the crawl is slow while the host is idle. Each cycle records documents/minute per shard, core count, load average and how many crawler processes are alive, then acts: restart a stopped shard when load is low, and report a measured concurrency recommendation (never raise concurrency on a guess - a first attempt at 16-way was measured slower than the serial version).
items.verify: docs/min, cores and load1 recorded every cycle; underuse stated with a number; a stopped shard restarted when the host is idle.
items.evidence: 2026-10-11T11:44:40+0200: 77.6 docs/min, load1 4.62/16 cores, 4 crawler process(es), 0 shard(s) stopped

items.title: Rebuild the graph and dense sidecars when the serving index generation changes
items.detail: The engine's extra lanes read sidecars (graph/entities.bin, vectors.bin) that go stale whenever the index is rebuilt. Both are rebuildable from the index alone, so this is additive: when the serving generation changes, run embed build then graph build detached and collect the result on a later cycle. A graph build over 19k documents measured 495 s, so it must never run inside a cycle.
items.verify: both sidecars exist and are newer than the generation they were built for; the generation is recorded in ops/state.json.
items.evidence: graph + dense sidecars rebuilt for generation 19254

items.title: Stop wasting the crawl on HTTP 429: back off per host and move on
items.detail: MEASURED: ~39,700 HTTP 429 responses across the four shards (10,412 shard 0, 10,187 shard 2, 9,736 shard 3, 9,358 shard 1) plus ~1,800 DNS failures - 76,349 error/timeout lines in total - while the box sits at load 3.8 of 16 cores and the fleet sustains only 52-94 docs/min. The crawler is spending its slots on hosts that are telling it to slow down. Fix in the fetcher/queue: honour Retry-After when present, back off exponentially per origin (not globally), and on a 429 move the slot to another origin instead of retrying the same one - host diversity is the resource we are not using. DNS failures must be counted and skipped, not retried forever. Keep the politeness guarantees: this must not become a way to hammer a host harder.
items.verify: after the change, a crawl window shows the 429 count falling as a share of responses and docs/min rising, with per-origin request rate never above the configured floor.

items.title: Raise CPU and RAM utilisation to the 80% target
items.detail: MEASURED 2026-10-11T11:44:40+0200: CPU 32.4% and RAM 25.4% against an 80% target; crawl 77.6 docs/min with 4 crawler process(es) on 16 cores; implied mean fetch latency 24.74 s
items.verify: CPU and RAM both at or above 80% on a sustained window, with throughput up and no host hammered past its configured rate.
